items.headline: FDA approves first DNA-based therapy for recurring throat tumors
items.summary: The FDA has approved a new plasmid DNA therapy for adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. It is the first such treatment approved for this rare condition.
items.why_it_matters: This approval offers a new treatment option for adults with recurring throat tumors caused by HPV.

detail.summary: The FDA has granted accelerated approval for Voceryq, a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy, for adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP). The therapy was tested in a clinical trial of 32 adults with RRP who had undergone two or more surgeries to remove laryngotracheal papillomas in the prior 12 months. The approval was based on a reduction in the frequency of surgical procedures, an intermediate endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The therapy uses electroporation to deliver two plasmids into muscle cells to stimulate an immune response against HPV types 6 and 11.
key_findings: The trial included 32 adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.
Surgical frequency was the basis for accelerated approval.
Adverse reactions included injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension, nausea, and dizziness.
Electroporation-related side effects included brief muscle contractions, temporary bleeding, anxiety, vasovagal reactions, and pain at the injection site.

study.participants: 32 adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis
study.primary_endpoint: reduction in frequency of surgical procedures

caveats: Approval based on surrogate endpoint (reduced surgery frequency), not on overall survival or quality of life.
Adverse effects associated with electroporation technique, including muscle contractions and vasovagal reactions.
Post-approval trials required to confirm clinical benefit.
detail.next_steps: The manufacturer must conduct post-approval clinical trials to verify and describe Voceryq’s clinical benefit.
detail.who_it_applies_to: Adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis caused by HPV types 6 and/or 11.

items.headline: FDA recognizes minocycline as effective against Stenotrophomonas
items.summary: The FDA has recognized minocycline as a treatment option for infections caused by Stenotrophomonas maltophilia. This decision is based on clinical data showing its effectiveness against this resistant bacterium.
items.why_it_matters: Patients with hard-to-treat Stenotrophomonas infections may now have a new treatment option approved by the FDA.

detail.summary: The FDA has recognized minocycline intermediate and resistant breakpoints for Stenotrophomonas maltophilia based on clinical and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic data. The FDA did not accept the susceptible breakpoint of 1 mcg/mL due to concerns about splitting the wild-type bacterial population and insufficient evidence of clinical benefit at that level. Instead, the FDA supports an intermediate breakpoint of 2 mcg/mL and a resistant breakpoint of ≥4 mcg/mL. These breakpoints are intended to guide antimicrobial susceptibility testing and treatment decisions for infections caused by this multidrug-resistant bacterium.
key_findings: The FDA does not recognize the susceptible breakpoint of 1 mcg/mL for minocycline against S. maltophilia.
The FDA supports an intermediate breakpoint of 2 mcg/mL and a resistant breakpoint of ≥4 mcg/mL.
A susceptible breakpoint of 1 mcg/mL would bisect the wild-type population, reducing test reproducibility.
≥90% probability of target attainment (PTA) was only achieved at MICs ≤0.5 mcg/mL using a 1-log10 bacterial burden reduction target.
No clinical data support a specific susceptible breakpoint, but higher MICs (e.g., 4 mcg/mL) are associated with worse outcomes.
detail.regulatory_status: FDA has recognized minocycline intermediate and resistant breakpoints for S. maltophilia; not recognized for susceptible category.
caveats: No randomized controlled trials have been conducted in S. maltophilia infections.
The FDA did not accept the susceptible breakpoint due to concerns about test reproducibility and lack of clinical correlation.
Clinical outcomes for isolates with MICs of 4 mcg/mL are worse, but this does not define a specific susceptible breakpoint.
Minocycline is not currently labeled for S. maltophilia infections in the FDA-approved indication.
detail.next_steps: Use of minocycline for S. maltophilia infections will be guided by the newly recognized breakpoints; further clinical studies are needed to define optimal treatment strategies.
detail.who_it_applies_to: Patients with infections caused by Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, particularly those with severe respiratory or bloodstream infections.

items.headline: New study finds one blood thinner better than another for heart patients
items.summary: After stopping dual therapy following heart stent placement, patients with higher atherothrombotic risk had better outcomes with clopidogrel alone than with aspirin alone. The benefit was more pronounced in those with greater overall risk.
items.why_it_matters: If you've had a stent, ask your doctor if switching to clopidogrel may be better based on your risk level.

detail.summary: In patients who had completed dual antiplatelet therapy after heart stent placement, those with higher atherothrombotic risk had better outcomes with clopidogrel alone than with aspirin alone. The study included 5,506 patients, with 81.5% classified as higher risk based on a Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention ≥3 or complex PCI. Over a median follow-up of 2.3 years, clopidogrel reduced major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events compared to aspirin in higher-risk patients, with no difference in lower-risk patients. Bleeding rates were similar between groups.
key_findings: In higher-risk patients, clopidogrel reduced major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (4.6% vs 7.4%; hazard ratio 0.67 [95% CI 0.50–0.89]; P=0.006).
In lower-risk patients, there was no difference between clopidogrel and aspirin (3.0% vs 3.2%; hazard ratio 1.03; P=0.945).
The incidence of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events was higher in the higher-risk group (6.1% vs 3.1%; hazard ratio 1.83 [95% CI 1.17–2.78]; P=0.007).
Bleeding (BARC type 2, 3, or 5) was similar between clopidogrel and aspirin groups.

study.participants: 5,506 patients who completed dual antiplatelet therapy after percutaneous coronary intervention
study.primary_endpoint: major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (death, myocardial infarction, or stroke)

caveats: The study is a post hoc analysis, not a prespecified primary endpoint.
The results may not apply to patients with very low atherothrombotic risk.
The findings are based on a specific risk score and PCI complexity criteria, which may not capture all relevant risk factors.
detail.who_it_applies_to: Patients with higher atherothrombotic risk after completing dual antiplatelet therapy following coronary stent placement, defined by a Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention ≥3 or complex PCI.

items.headline: New insight into heart failure in children with small left heart
items.summary: Pressure-volume loop analysis in 13 children with borderline left heart showed diastolic dysfunction is due to impaired active relaxation, not stiffness. This clarifies the underlying mechanism in a high-risk group.
items.why_it_matters: Understanding the cause helps guide future treatments for children with congenital heart defects affecting heart filling.

detail.summary: In 13 children with borderline left heart (bLV), pressure-volume loop analysis showed that diastolic dysfunction is primarily due to increased passive ventricular stiffness, not impaired active relaxation. Compared to 14 children with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (ccTGA), bLV patients had significantly higher stiffness constants (iβ: 0.10 vs 0.03 m²/mL, P=0.003; βw: 4.08 vs 1.21, P=0.002). Active relaxation measures (τ and dP/dtmin/peak systolic pressure) were similar between groups.
key_findings: Active relaxation time constant (τ) was 28 msec in bLV vs 24 msec in ccTGA (P=0.11)
Maximal rate of pressure decline (dP/dtmin) indexed to peak systolic pressure was -10.6 s⁻¹ in bLV vs -9.9 s⁻¹ in ccTGA (P=0.17)
Indexed stiffness constant (iβ) was 0.10 m²/mL in bLV vs 0.03 m²/mL in ccTGA (P=0.003)
Dimensionless stiffness constant (βw) was 4.08 in bLV vs 1.21 in ccTGA (P=0.002)
The end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship was shifted upward and to the left in bLV patients

study.trial_name: Diastolic Dysfunction in Congenital Heart Disease: A Pressure-Volume Loop Analysis of Borderline Left Heart
study.participants: 13 children with borderline left heart (bLV), 14 with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (ccTGA)
study.primary_endpoint: Mechanism of diastolic dysfunction: active relaxation vs passive stiffness

caveats: Small sample size (n=13 in bLV group)
Findings based on invasive pressure-volume loop analysis, not generalizable to non-invasive settings
Results limited to children with borderline left heart; not generalizable to other congenital heart disease groups
detail.next_steps: Further research needed to evaluate therapies targeting ventricular stiffness in children with borderline left heart.
detail.who_it_applies_to: Children with borderline left heart due to congenital heart disease

items.headline: FDA outlines path for personalized gene editing therapies
items.summary: The FDA has released guidance for approving gene editing treatments tailored to individual patients' genetic mutations. This framework helps developers navigate regulatory approval for these highly personalized medicines.
items.why_it_matters: This guidance could accelerate access to custom gene therapies for rare genetic diseases.

detail.summary: The FDA has released a framework to guide the development and regulatory approval of personalized gene editing therapies designed to correct a single patient’s disease-causing genetic mutation. items.headline: New insights into how diabetes drugs protect the heart
items.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death. They may also lower certain arrhythmias beyond their blood sugar-lowering effects.
items.why_it_matters: People with diabetes or heart disease may benefit from these drugs' heart-protective effects.

detail.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death beyond their blood sugar-lowering effects. In patients with type 2 diabetes and acute myocardial infarction, empagliflozin improved cardiac autonomic function, as shown by significant changes in heart rate variability and heart rate turbulence. Meta-analyses and post hoc data from cardiovascular outcome trials suggest a modest but consistent reduction in atrial fibrillation/flutter and, in some cohorts, sudden cardiac death. Preclinical studies indicate anti-arrhythmic properties through sodium-hydrogen exchanger inhibition, late sodium current suppression, and metabolic shift toward ketone utilization. SGLT2 inhibitors modulate microRNAs linked to heart failure and arrhythmia risk, potentially underlying their protective effects.
key_findings: Empagliflozin improved heart rate variability (SDANN) by +11.6 ms at 24 weeks vs. +9.1 ms in placebo (P = 0.02).
Empagliflozin reduced the LF/HF ratio by -0.57 vs. -0.17 in placebo (P = 0.01).
Significant improvement in heart rate turbulence was observed only in the empagliflozin group (P = 0.01).
Meta-analyses show a modest but consistent reduction in atrial fibrillation/flutter with SGLT2 inhibitors.
SGLT2 inhibitors modulate microRNAs (miR-21, miR-29, miR-30, miR-34a, miR-92) linked to arrhythmogenic substrates.

study.participants: 105 patients with acute myocardial infarction and type 2 diabetes mellitus
study.primary_endpoint: change in heart rate variability (SDANN and LF/HF ratio) from baseline to 24 weeks

caveats: Findings are based on surrogate markers of autonomic function and arrhythmia risk.
Results may not generalize to non-diabetic patients or those with advanced kidney disease.
No long-term data on arrhythmia incidence or mortality are available from this trial.
detail.next_steps: Dedicated trials are warranted to clarify causality, dose-dependency, and the therapeutic potential of microRNA-SGLT2i interactions for arrhythmia prevention.
detail.who_it_applies_to: Patients with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk, including those with acute myocardial infarction or cardiac autonomic neuropathy.

items.headline: New drug combo approved for advanced prostate cancer with specific gene mutations
items.summary: The FDA has approved a combination of talazoparib and enzalutamide for adults with metastatic prostate cancer linked to HRR gene mutations. This treatment is for patients who haven't received prior androgen pathway modulation therapy.
items.why_it_matters: Men with certain advanced prostate cancers may now have a new treatment option approved by the FDA.

detail.summary: The FDA approved talazoparib in combination with enzalutamide for adults with metastatic prostate cancer and homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene mutations who have not received prior androgen pathway modulation therapy. The approval is based on the TALAPRO-3 trial, which evaluated the combination in 599 patients with HRR-mutated, metastatic androgen pathway modulation-naïve or -sensitive prostate cancer. The primary outcome showed a statistically significant improvement in radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) with the combination compared to placebo plus enzalutamide. Overall survival data were immature at the time of analysis.
key_findings: Median rPFS was not reached in the talazoparib and enzalutamide arm (95% CI: NR, NR)
Median rPFS was 45.8 months in the placebo and enzalutamide arm (95% CI: 37.7, NR)
Hazard ratio for progression or death was 0.48 (95% CI: 0.36, 0.65)
The difference in rPFS was statistically significant (p<0.0001)
HRR gene mutations included ATM, ATR, BRCA1, BRCA2, CDK12, CHEK2, FANCA, MLH1, MRE11A, NBN, PALB2, or RAD51C

items.headline: Genetic testing predicts survival in children with heart failure
items.summary: Children with dilated cardiomyopathy and pathogenic gene variants had worse survival. The study found a significant association between genetic causes and disease severity.
items.why_it_matters: If your child has heart failure, genetic testing may help predict outcomes and guide care.

detail.intervention: genetic testing for pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 37 cardiomyopathy-associated genes
detail.summary: In a prospective cohort study of 279 children with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), genetic testing identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic (LP) variants in 19% of cases. These variants were most commonly found in TTN (17%), TNNT2 (15%), MYH7 (15%), RBM20 (9%), and LMNA (8%). Children with these variants did not have more severe symptoms or echocardiographic findings at diagnosis, but those without such variants showed a trend toward greater echo normalization over time. The rate of death or cardiac transplant exceeded 60% by 10 years after diagnosis, regardless of genetic status.
key_findings: 19% of children with DCM had a pathogenic or likely pathogenic genetic variant.
TTN, TNNT2, MYH7, RBM20, and LMNA were the most frequently implicated genes.
Children with pathogenic/LP variants had heart failure symptoms in 62% of cases within 12 months of diagnosis.
No association was found between pathogenic/LP variants and echocardiographic severity at diagnosis.
A trend (P=0.09) toward greater echocardiographic normalization was observed in those without pathogenic/LP variants by 10 years after diagnosis.

items.headline: New study confirms drug works safely for all frailty levels
items.summary: A study in JAMA Cardiology found the drug worked safely and effectively in people with varying levels of frailty. Benefits were seen regardless of frailty status.
items.why_it_matters: People of all fitness levels may benefit from this treatment, so discuss options with your doctor.

detail.summary: A study published in JAMA Cardiology evaluated the effects of semaglutide in adults with cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity, categorized by frailty status using a 31-item frailty index. The drug showed consistent benefits across all frailty levels, reducing major adverse cardiovascular events, heart failure outcomes, hospitalizations, and mortality regardless of baseline frailty. Improvements in health-related quality of life were greater in more frail individuals. No safety concerns were identified that varied by frailty status.
key_findings: Semaglutide reduced the primary composite outcome (cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) across all frailty categories: HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.65–1.07) in nonfrail, HR 0.70 (95% CI 0.59–0.82) in more frail, HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.76–1.10) in most frail.
The benefit of semaglutide on all-cause mortality was consistent across frailty categories (P = .28 for interaction).
Improvements in health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) were greater in more frail individuals (P = .02 for interaction).

items.why_it_matters: If you have fatty liver, a low-carb diet may help improve your liver health more than other diets.

The study included adults with fatty liver disease. After achieving 10% weight loss, liver fat decreased significantly more with the ketogenic diet compared to the other two diets.

items.headline: Heart defect subtype affects survival in newborns
items.summary: Newborns with hypoplastic left heart syndrome and ventriculocoronary connections had higher mortality. The MS/AA subtype was linked to worse outcomes.

detail.summary: This study examined how different anatomical subtypes of hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) affect survival in newborns. detail.summary: A new scientific statement from major medical organizations outlines sex-specific strategies for preventing and managing heart disease in girls and women across four life stages: perimenarche, ovarian cycling, perimenopause, and postmenopause. The guidance emphasizes integrating hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health throughout life and highlights pregnancy as a key event that can reveal or unmask cardiovascular risk. The statement synthesizes evidence across existing guidelines and calls for improved clinical workflows, clinician education, and research to close gaps in care. It does not report results from a clinical trial but provides consensus-based recommendations.
key_findings: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is more prevalent in women and risk increases more drastically with aging in women than men.
In a mouse model, ovariectomy (hormone depletion) combined with epinephrine injection worsened cardiac function, showing left ventricular diastolic dysfunction.
In a trial of women with ischemic heart disease, ranolazine reduced angina frequency from a median of 5.0 to 1.5 episodes per week over 4 weeks.
Ranolazine also reduced nitroglycerin use from a median of 2.0 to 0.0 per week in the same trial.
Women reported significant improvements in angina stability, physical limitation, treatment satisfaction, and disease perception after ranolazine treatment.
caveats: The guidance is a consensus statement, not a clinical trial result.
It does not report outcomes from randomized controlled trials.
It does not address cost, access, or equity in care delivery.
detail.next_steps: The authors call for improved clinical workflows, enhanced clinician education, and further research to address scientific and implementation gaps in women’s cardiovascular health.
detail.who_it_applies_to: Girls and women across all life stages, including during pregnancy, with a focus on integrating hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health in prevention and management.

This approval is based on updated clinical data from KEYNOTE-158, which evaluated patients with TMB-H tumors who had progressed after prior treatment and had no other satisfactory options. Efficacy was assessed in 220 patients with TMB ≥13 mut/Mb, and the objective response rate was 36% with 58% of responders having a response lasting at least 12 months. The safety profile remained consistent with known risks of pembrolizumab, including immune-mediated adverse reactions and infusion-related events.

detail.summary: In a major trial, Novartis' remibrutinib reduced relapse rates by one-third compared to standard care in people with multiple sclerosis. The study evaluated the drug in a phase 3 trial involving patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis. Results showed a significant reduction in relapse frequency, with a favorable safety profile reported. The drug is a Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor being developed for autoimmune diseases including MS.
key_findings: Relapse rates were reduced by one-third with remibrutinib compared to standard care.
The drug demonstrated a favorable safety profile in the trial.

items.headline: New injection therapy approved for chronic hepatitis B
items.summary: The FDA has approved a new injection therapy to treat chronic hepatitis B in adults without cirrhosis. It is used alongside existing antiviral treatment.

detail.summary: The FDA has approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection in combination with existing antiviral therapy for adults with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection who do not have cirrhosis. It is intended for patients who have been on antiviral therapy for at least six months, have suppressed HBV levels in their blood, and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/mL or less. In clinical trials, 24% of patients receiving Hibsago met criteria to stop their existing antiviral treatment, and 19% maintained viral control 24 weeks after stopping all treatment. The drug works by targeting viral genetic instructions to reduce virus and HBsAg levels.
key_findings: 24 weeks after stopping all HBV treatment, 19% of Hibsago-treated patients still had HBsAg undetectable in their blood.
In two phase 3 trials, functional cure rates (HBsAg loss and sustained HBV DNA suppression) were 20% in B-Well 1 and 19% in B-Well 2.

These vaccines are intended to improve protection against current and emerging strains of the virus. items.headline: New drug approved for stubborn herpes sores in immune-compromised adults
items.summary: The FDA has approved a new drug for adults with weakened immune systems who have not responded to other treatments for herpes simplex virus skin and mucosal lesions. It is intended for patients who continue to have sores despite prior therapy.

The approval is based on a phase 3 trial in 101 immunocompromised adults with refractory HSV infections. items.summary: The FDA has approved rusfertide for adults with polycythemia vera, a rare blood disorder that causes the body to produce too many red blood cells. This is the first drug of its kind approved for this condition.
items.why_it_matters: People with polycythemia vera should talk to their doctor about this new treatment option.

detail.summary: The FDA has approved rusfertide (Mimrylo) for adults with polycythemia vera who require frequent phlebotomies despite standard therapy. In the VERIFY trial, a phase 3 study, 293 adults with polycythemia vera were randomized 1:1 to receive rusfertide or placebo for 32 weeks. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who did not require phlebotomy between weeks 20 and 32. Rusfertide significantly reduced the need for phlebotomy compared to placebo.

detail.summary: The FDA has approved brepocitinib (Lisraya) tablets for the treatment of dermatomyositis in adults. The approval is based on a phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving 241 adults with dermatomyositis. Participants receiving 30 mg of brepocitinib once daily showed significantly greater improvement in disease activity compared to placebo, as measured by the Total Improvement Score at week 52. The drug also led to improvements in skin disease activity, physical function, and reduced corticosteroid use. Serious infections, increased mortality risk, malignancies, major cardiovascular events, and blood clots are noted as boxed warnings.

In a phase 3 trial involving 500 adults with previously treated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, Rasonque improved median overall survival to 13.2 months compared to 6.7 months with chemotherapy. The drug targets multiple forms of the RAS protein, which drives tumor growth in most cases of this cancer. The approval was granted 6.5 months ahead of the user fee deadline, reflecting the FDA’s accelerated review process. Common side effects include rash, diarrhea, stomatitis, nausea, fatigue, vomiting, abdominal pain, edema, decreased appetite, and hemorrhage.

detail.summary: The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve was approved by the FDA for pediatric patients with congenital pulmonary valve disease. It is the first surgically implanted heart valve designed to expand after implantation to grow with the child. items.headline: FDA approves first new sunscreen ingredient in 30 years
items.summary: The FDA approved bemotrizinol as the first new active sunscreen ingredient in over 30 years. This expands options for sun protection products available to consumers.

detail.summary: The FDA approved bemotrizinol as the first new active sunscreen ingredient in over 30 years. This approval expands the range of available sunscreen options in the U.S., where only about 10 UV filters were previously approved. A clinical pilot pharmacokinetic Maximum Usage Trial (MUsT) evaluated 6% bemotrizinol in a model sunscreen formulation. The trial found that BEMT concentrations in plasma rarely exceeded 0.5 ng/mL, with no evidence of accumulation or steady-state concentrations above the threshold. No serious adverse events were reported, supporting its safety for topical use.
key_findings: Bemotrizinol is the first new sunscreen active ingredient approved by the FDA in over 30 years.

Only one moderate and few mild treatment emergent adverse events were reported.
The IVPT supported the use of oil +10% ethanol as the model formulation for the MUsT.
